item.title: A five-euro 'toll': Europe shouldn't be penny-wise and pound-foolish: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03 00:23:00
Photo taken on September 3, 2026 shows e-commerce parcels stored at a warehouse near Liege Airport in Grace-Hollogne, Belgium. Photo: VCG The five-euro charge needs to be viewed in the context of the overall scale of China-EU trade. The nature of this policy is even more worthy of deep consideration. Such a penny-wise, pound-foolish approach may appear to bolster government coffers in the short term, but it comes at the expense of Europe's long-term economic vitality. It will also create unnecessary friction in the mutually beneficial economic and trade relationship between China and the EU, ultimately harming Europe's own development interests. The European Union (EU) has imposed a so-called two-euro "handling fee" on packages from outside the bloc to European consumers since Sunday. Combined with the three-euro charge introduced in July on small packages worth less than 150 euros, this new revenue-grabbing levy brings the fixed customs-clearance costs on a low-value parcel to five euros. What's more, the handling fee will be levied separately for each category of goods in the same parcel. For example, if a parcel contains three categories of goods, the handling fee will amount to six euros, regardless of how many items fall into each category. Given that approximately 93 percent of cheap packages that entered the EU came from China, the move is widely seen as being clearly targeted at Chinese goods. The five-euro charge needs to be viewed in the context of the overall scale of China-EU trade. More importantly, the nature of this policy is even more worthy of deep consideration. The figures tell a revealing story: 5.9 billion parcels annually, a fixed charge of three to five euros per package, and an annual revenue boost of six billion euros for the EU budget. Combined with the rule allowing fees to accumulate across different product categories, this measure has gone well beyond the traditional role of tariffs in regulating trade. It effectively amounts to an "entry tax" imposed on consumers even before they complete their purchases. Europe once built its identity on free trade. Yet it is now turning into an economy that charges tolls at its own doorstep, parcel by parcel. The more lucrative this toll-collecting business becomes, the further Europe drifts from its original principles. The money may flow into EU coffers, but ordinary European consumers will bear the costs. The EU claims that the new fee will be paid by platforms and sellers. However, e-commerce platform AliExpress has explicitly warned that the charges would hurt low-income households in Europe and "exacerbate the cost-of-living crisis." The European Consumer Organisation (BEUC) has also expressed concern that some platforms may try to pass these new costs onto consumers at the final stages of the purchase. A three-euro trinket subject to an additional five euros in charges would end up costing more in taxes than the product itself. It is clear whom this kind of measure is really "protecting." A new wave of protests is currently spreading across Europe. Although the specific demands vary, protesters share common concerns over inadequate public investment and the rising cost of living. The EU's decision to introduce a "toll" on small parcels is, in essence, an attempt to shift its fiscal anxieties onto ordinary citizens through administrative measures. Imposing additional charges on low-value parcels amid high inflation will hit European consumers even harder, and will exacerbate mounting tensions over people's livelihoods and further inflame already strained public sentiment. At a deeper level, such a short-sighted policy choice exposes Europe's strategic confusion amid profound changes in the global economic and trade landscape. Faced with the rapid growth of cross-border e-commerce and the competitive advantages brought about by China's industrial upgrading, Europe has chosen not to address these challenges by strengthening its own industrial competitiveness and improving the efficiency of its internal market. Instead, it has reverted to the old path of trade protectionism, using administrative barriers to fragment global supply chains. This approach not only runs counter to the free trade principles Europe has long championed but also undermines its credibility in shaping global economic and trade rules. Such a penny-wise, pound-foolish approach may appear to bolster government coffers in the short term, but it comes at the expense of Europe's long-term economic vitality. It will also create unnecessary friction in the mutually beneficial economic and trade relationship between China and the EU, ultimately harming Europe's own development interests. Tariff barriers cannot resolve Europe's structural problems. The price advantages of Chinese e-commerce stem from the efficiency of its industrial and supply chains, rather than merely from a tax exemption policy. The EU may be able to keep goods out of its market, but it cannot make its domestic supply chains equally efficient overnight. Some European business representatives have put the calculation more bluntly: US tariff hikes have already pushed up the price of European wines in North America by 15 to 25 percent compared with three years ago. Now, with procurement costs from China rising as well, some European buyers are turning to US platforms instead. "Who is the ultimate winner? American companies." In stark contrast to this wall-building approach lies another path to development. China-EU trade and investment consultations have yielded multiple results, BYD's factory in Hungary is set to begin mass production, the China-Switzerland free trade agreement has been upgraded, and China's hybrid car exports to the EU surged by more than 200 percent year on year in September. On the same continent, two different choices are producing two different outcomes: those building walls are reaping anxiety, while those embracing openness are securing orders. The small-parcel levy is just one of several restrictive measures introduced by the EU this year. Europe was once among the champions of free trade, yet it is now "closing" its doors through measures that amount to squeezing every last penny out of consumers. Genuine competitiveness is forged through market competition. Translating anxiety into tax rates will only cause Europe to fall further behind amid the technological revolution, while forcing ordinary households to foot the bill for political maneuvering. China and the EU are important economic and trade partners. And China maintains that an open and inclusive international trading environment serves the common interests of all parties. Whether Europe chooses to narrow that door further or open it again is a question whose answer is already clear.

item.title: Xi holds talks with Sultan of Oman, calls for deeper alignment, regional peace
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03 00:04:00
Chinese President Xi Jinping holds talks with Sultan Haitham Bin Tarik Al Said of Oman, who is on a state visit to China, at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, capital of China, Nov. 2, 2026. (Photo: Xinhua) Chinese President Xi Jinping held talks with Sultan Haitham Bin Tarik Al Said of Oman in Beijing on Monday, with the two sides exchanging views on bilateral relations as well as international and regional hotspot issues. The Chinese leader said that China stands ready to deepen the alignment of development strategies with Oman, while also emphasizing that the Middle East and the Gulf region should not become a wrestling ground for major-country rivalry and geopolitical conflicts, the Xinhua News Agency reported. Following the talks, the two heads of state witnessed the signing of cooperation documents in areas including the application of the BeiDou Navigation Satellite System, industrial and supply chains, green development, currency swaps, digital payments, and digital currencies. During the visit, the two sides issued a joint statement on deepening the China-Oman strategic partnership. Under the statement, the two sides will strengthen political mutual trust, intensify friendly exchanges, expand mutually beneficial cooperation and enhance coordination and collaboration. They call for resolving differences through political and diplomatic means and encourage the US and Iran to pursue peaceful options. They consider it necessary to restore normal and safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and agree to maintain communication on matters concerning the Strait, according to the Foreign Ministry of Oman. Sultan Haitham's state visit, which lasted from November 1 to 2, marks the first visit to China by an Omani head of state since diplomatic ties were established in 1978. Analysts note that the visit represents a full upgrade of China-Oman ties, steering practical bilateral cooperation toward greater diversification, stability and sustainability. At a time of heightened tensions in the Middle East, the visit carries constructive significance for upholding regional peace and stability and safeguarding the security of international shipping lanes. For regional states, closer cooperation with China has become an inevitable and preferred option. Opening new opportunities During the meeting with Sultan Haitham, Xi said that China stands ready to deepen the alignment of development strategies with Oman, turning the two countries into stable and reliable partners in energy, partners with great potential in investment, and partners in high-tech innovation. According to Wang Jin, an associate professor at the Institute of Middle Eastern Studies at Northwest University in Xi'an, Sultan Haitham's state visit marks a full upgrade of China-Oman relations amid deepening political trust and strategic cooperation. The bilateral progress is not directed at any third party nor driven by geopolitical contests. Instead, both sides aim to inject more positive energy into regional peace and stability by advancing cooperation, showcasing the open and constructive nature of China's engagement with Middle Eastern states, said Wang. China and Oman established a strategic partnership in 2018. Currently, China is Oman's largest trading partner, and Oman is China's fourth largest trading partner among Arab states, according to the Chinese Foreign Ministry. Official data shows that bilateral trade between China and Oman hit $32.87 billion in 2025. China mainly exports machinery and electrical goods, steel products, high-tech items and textiles to Oman and is the largest buyer of Omani crude oil, with imports standing at 35.353 million tonnes in 2025. China and Oman enjoy strong economic and trade complementarity, and bilateral cooperation is expanding beyond traditional energy trade into more areas, said Wang. Oman is a major energy producer and international trade hub in the Gulf. China, with its ultra-large market, complete industrial system and strong infrastructure capacity, boasts notable strengths in equipment manufacturing, communications and new energy, which can underpin Oman's economic diversification and industrialization, he added. Zhu Yongbiao, an expert on Middle East affairs at Lanzhou University, told the Global Times that the two sides enjoy broad prospects for cooperation spanning green energy transition, the digital economy, artificial intelligence, port logistics and supply chain development, as well as science, education and talent training. Such efforts will steer China-Oman economic and trade ties toward a more diversified, stable and sustainable pattern, Zhu noted. In a Sunday article prior to the top-level engagement in Beijing, the Oman Observer noted that the visit marks "a landmark in Omani-Chinese relations." The visit carries a particular importance in light of the steady evolution of bilateral ties and the wider horizon it holds for deepening the strategic partnership, and it opens the way for closer cooperation across political, economic, investment, cultural and scientific fields, the media outlet said. A natural regional preference Sultan Haitham's state visit to China takes place amid simmering tensions in the Middle East. The protracted US-Iran standoff and spillover of the Yemen conflict have intertwined risks in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, posing grave threats to shipping security and the global energy supply chain. When holding talks with Sultan Haitham, President Xi said that China is willing to enhance communication and coordination with Arab countries and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries including Oman for the early restoration of regional peace and tranquility and the realization of lasting stability, according to Xinhua. He noted that the Middle East and the Gulf region should not become a wrestling ground for major-country rivalry and geopolitical conflicts, and that regional peace and stability requires the joint efforts and care of all parties. Sultan Haitham said Oman highly appreciates China's just position on the Middle East issue and stands ready to maintain close coordination with China to uphold international law, advocate for the peaceful resolution of disputes, and jointly promote security and stability in the region and beyond. Regarding the Middle Eastern security, China has been committed to stopping the war and contributing wisdom and solutions to resolving the region's security dilemmas. On Monday, China's top diplomat Wang Yi met with Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council (SNSC) in Beijing. The Chinese Foreign Ministry announced that China will send several special envoys to countries in the Middle East, the Red Sea region and the Horn of Africa in November to promote dialogue and help ease regional tensions. During the meeting with Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, in Beijing in April, President Xi put forward a four-point proposal on promoting peace and stability in the Middle East. In his talks with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi in Cairo this September, the Chinese leader raised a four-point proposal on building a new security architecture in the Middle East via upholding a vision of common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security. "Strategically located on the southern flank of the Strait of Hormuz and linked to the Red Sea and Yemen, Oman follows a balanced, pragmatic diplomacy and acts as a vital mediator between Gulf states, Iran and Western powers," said Zhu, "As a permanent member of the UN Security Council, China also maintains sound cooperation with Middle Eastern countries." The meeting between the Chinese and Omani leaders facilitates strategic communication and the alignment of positions on regional situations, enabling the two sides to work together to de-escalate tensions, said Wang. "It carries constructive significance for maintaining regional peace and stability and protecting the security of international shipping routes," he said, adding that shipping security ultimately depends on the overall de-escalation of regional tensions and the collective efforts of all relevant parties, and calls for joint endeavors from the international community. Against the backdrop of protracted regional conflicts and rising uncertainties in global energy and trade, the succession of high-level visits to China by Middle Eastern countries shows that they generally value China's strategic weight and influence in international affairs, as well as development opportunities brought by its market, industrial system and scientific and technological innovation, said Wang Jin. Regional countries hope to foster a more stable and enabling external environment for their own development through deeper cooperation with China, he added. According to Zhu, China adheres to non-interference in internal affairs, rejects bloc confrontation and seeks no geopolitical gains. China's approach to cooperation on trade, energy, non-traditional security and regional hotspot issues is stable, constructive and dynamic. "For Middle Eastern countries, strengthening cooperation with China has become an inevitable and preferred option," he noted.

item.title: Open source and practical AI take center stage at Wuzhen Summit
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-02 23:58:00
At the 2026 "Light of the Internet" Expo, a flagship event of the World Internet Conference (WIC) Wuzhen Summit in Jiaxing, East China's Zhejiang Province, visitors experience robotic vending services and explore new scenarios of smart consumption on November 2, 2026. Photo: VCG From robots filling prescriptions at smart pharmacies to automated systems handling garment sewing and precision assembly on factory floors, and sixth-generation (6G) mobile communications enabling the remote operation of construction machinery, futuristic applications were on display at the 2026 "Light of the Internet" Expo, which opened on Monday in Wuzhen, East China's Zhejiang Province. As a flagship event of the World Internet Conference (WIC) Wuzhen Summit, the expo highlighted China's accelerating efforts to integrate artificial intelligence (AI) and other cutting-edge technologies into real-world industrial and everyday applications, as well as its commitment to global cooperation in emerging technologies, Chinese analysts said. From November 2 to 5, the 2026 World Internet Conference (WIC) Wuzhen Summit has brought global attention back to this water town in East China. Under the theme "Open Source and Openness, Joint Contribution and Shared Benefits - Jointly Building a Community with a Shared Future in Cyberspace," the summit convenes government officials, representatives from international organizations, tech executives and researchers from around the world. Chinese industry experts and WIC participants noted that, with global AI development increasingly split between open-source and closed-source approaches, this year's WIC theme is especially significant. It demonstrates China's commitment to global AI cooperation and its willingness to engage with partners worldwide. The "Light of the Internet" Expo, which opened on Monday, features 671 companies and institutions across 54 countries and regions, showcasing over 1,000 new technological achievements. The six themed exhibition areas span communications infrastructure, computing capabilities, manufacturing, everyday services and cybersecurity. A number of cutting-edge technologies and products are making their debut at the expo, including satellite internet and 6G mobile communications, the Global Times learned. Open source goes tangible A major highlight of this year's summit is that "open source" has evolved from a concept into something tangible and interactive. For the first time, the WIC has invited developers under 40 to debate how open models can address real industrial needs. Xiang Ligang, president of the Beijing Institute of Intelligent Era Industry, told the Global Times on Monday that global AI development is now forming two distinct paths, with the US tending toward closed-source approaches, where major tech companies operate separately and form "silos" that hinder further progress. Against this backdrop, the WIC's theme of open source and shared benefits reflects China's commitment to and confidence in its own path - promoting openness and open source while advancing AI models, data and talent in a coordinated manner. "AI ultimately needs to become a powerful service system integrating society-wide cloud infrastructure, data centers, talent and communications; no single company can do this alone," Xiang said. "Only through open source and openness can capabilities be integrated to connect all aspects of social life and deliver real service value." AI-powered productivity As Monday's expo showcased China's advances in AI and its expanding industrial applications, along with emerging opportunities for global cooperation, Liu Dingding, a Chinese technology industry analyst, told the Global Times that the focus of the WIC is shifting from demonstrating technological capabilities to showing how AI can serve real production and benefit everyday needs. Alibaba, Huawei, ZTE and Sugon have brought computing super-node systems to the expo, alongside displays exploring advances in multimodal AI and spatial intelligence. Schneider Electric's exhibits cover production and inspection applications in semiconductor manufacturing, new-energy batteries, and electronic components. A future factory exhibition area features flexible garment sewing and precision component assembly, with humanoid robots like Aitu - designed for garment manufacturing - exploring applications in flexible production, the Global Times learned from the WIC's organizer. The data behind the host town itself tells a compelling story. On the eve of the first Wuzhen Summit, the town could identify only 12 internet-related enterprises. By 2024, that number had surpassed 1,200 - a hundredfold increase. Wuzhen's GDP grew from 2.84 billion yuan ($426 million) to 10.89 billion yuan, effectively "rebuilding three Wuzhens." Chinese cybersecurity firm DBAPP Security demonstrated its X security digital employees at the expo. These products are designed to undertake penetration testing, code auditing, security operations, and managed security services. The company said that the digital employees translate security specialists' knowledge and working methods into agents capable of planning and executing tasks, providing round-the-clock services with capacity that can be expanded according to customer demand. The WIC's sub-forum agenda reflects the same industrial orientation. Across 27 sessions, topics range from agent interoperability to embodied intelligence, spatio-temporal intelligence and green, low-carbon transitions. Global AI cooperation for shared gains International participation remains high, with Intel, Qualcomm, Microsoft, Schneider Electric and Kaspersky among the exhibitors. Their displays cover computing chips, communications, software, smart manufacturing, and cybersecurity. Liu said that opportunities for international cooperation lie in technologies that can meet concrete needs across industries, including chips, memory, and robotics. He cited advanced driver assistance systems that combine overseas chips with Chinese lidar and algorithms as an example of how complementary capabilities can support wider deployment. The WIC comes at a time when some countries are trying to erect protectionist walls and form exclusive circles in an area that thrives on global exchanges and cooperation At the just concluded Quad foreign ministers' meeting, the grouping expressed its intention to provide more than $85 million in technical and financial assistance to support access to trusted AI technologies across the so-called "Indo-Pacific." Chinese experts said that AI's future will not be decided by a few countries alone, but by whether the tools are interoperable, accountable and affordable. He Weiwen, a senior fellow at the Center for China and Globalization, said global AI cooperation should be built under a multilateral framework with the aim of achieving shared benefits for all countries, and warned that seeking exclusive groupings in digital technologies would incur not only immediate economic costs but also weaken global AI cooperation. Over the years, the theme of the WIC has evolved from internet to internet plus communication and now to AI, the development of which is not a matter for any single country and requires global coordination and shared rules to prosper. "In this context, the WIC's role as a communication platform has continued to strengthen, helping attract global participation and promote common standards and rules for safety and mutual understanding. One single conference cannot solve all the problems, but the summit provides an important platform and channel," Xiang said.

item.title: GT Voice: What will open the door to $1t export club for S.Korea, others?
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-02 23:02:00
A view of SK hynix's headquarters building in Icheon, Gyeonggi Province, South Korea, on October 28, 2026. Photo: VCG The artificial intelligence (AI) boom is propelling South Korea toward a $1 trillion export milestone. Its exports totaled $930 billion in the first 10 months of the year, putting the country on track to become the fourth nation, after the US, China and Germany, to surpass $1 trillion in annual exports, the Seoul Economic Daily reported on Monday. What lies behind South Korea's bid to join the $1 trillion export club? Several factors are at play, but one deserves particular attention: the global AI boom. International discussions of AI sometimes focus on the contest for technological leadership. Yet the economic demand stemming from the rapid development of AI deserves far greater attention. This demand is helping South Korea knock on the door of the $1 trillion export club. The force of AI demand is clearly visible in South Korea's October export figures. Semiconductor exports jumped 259.4 percent to $56.44 billion, reflecting continued heavy investment by global technology companies in the AI industry. Computer exports soared 496.6 percent to $5.85 billion, as the spread of AI services drove greater investment in server infrastructure. Electrical equipment exports increased 74 percent to $1.99 billion, reflecting rising demand for transformers, wires, cables, and other equipment used in AI data centers. These figures point to a much bigger story. The global expansion of AI is generating enormous demand across industries. This is a powerful new source of growth for manufacturers and exporters around the world. The 2025 World Trade Report issued by the World Trade Organization (WTO) estimates that with the right enabling policies, AI could boost the value of cross-border flows of goods and services by nearly 40 percent by 2040, thanks to productivity gains and lower trade costs. South Korea's export figures raise two broader questions. First, can the country cross the $1 trillion threshold and sustain that level of exports? Second, could more economies join the club in the years ahead? The WTO's projections offer grounds for considering both possibilities. If AI continues to fuel global trade growth, the $1 trillion export club may have more members in the years ahead. To tap into this demand, it is first necessary to understand what drives it. AI is not a single product or industry, but a complex, layered system built on semiconductors, data, computing infrastructure, energy, models and applications. South Korea's export figures offer a glimpse of just how finely specialized this supply chain has become. Alongside chips and computers, exports include transformers, wires, cables and other equipment needed to power and operate AI data centers. These components and capabilities are closely interconnected, linking companies and economies in a global network of production and trade. Within this global network, China is becoming an increasingly important market as its AI industry advances rapidly. South Korea's trade figures offer a telling example. In October, its exports to China rose 133.6 percent to $26.98 billion, with semiconductors and wireless communication devices among the major export items. China's expanding technology sector is generating demand that reaches beyond its borders. That picture is difficult to reconcile with claims that China's demand is faltering. In September, China's imports grew at a double-digit rate, while exports also continued to expand. As China's technology exports grow, it continues to import goods, creating opportunities for suppliers in other economies. This two-way trade makes China an important participant in the expansion of global trade in the AI era. For South Korea to sustain its export growth, deeper integration into global supply chains and open trade will matter. The same applies to other economies seeking to join the $1 trillion export club. The WTO's World Trade Report emphasizes the importance of an open and predictable trading environment in ensuring that the benefits of AI are widely shared. For South Korea and other economies looking to expand their exports, deeper integration into global supply chains, stronger industrial cooperation and support for open trade may be the keys to unlocking the door to the $1 trillion export club.

item.title: US heads into midterm elections, 'result may sway Mideast trajectories'
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-02 22:56:00
Americans cast their ballots at an early voting station in Seattle, the US, on November 1, 2026 local time, ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 Senate seats are up for contest. Photo: IC Americans will head to polling stations on November 3 for midterm elections, the result of which will decide congressional control for the next two years. Republicans are fighting political history, as the party in power in Washington has traditionally lost seats during midterm election years. The GOP also faces a challenging political climate fueled by persistent inflation tied in part to war with Iran and increasingly negative approval ratings of the US President, according to Fox News on Sunday. Trump held campaign rallies in Salina, Kansas and Dubuque, Iowa on Sunday. An Associated Press report said these trips reflect the GOP's "defensive posture." It noted that "This year, Trump has focused largely on states he has dominated before as voters, including previous supporters, question the economic fallout of his decision to impose tariffs and launch the war in Iran." But the BBC reported that there are a number of reasons why Democrats may not have as good a night as history might suggest or as some might expect. Firstly, much of the territory in play in this election Trump conquered with ease in the presidential election just two years ago. It's like a home game for Republicans. Then there have been changes to House election boundaries over the years that have meant fewer seats switch between parties. Thirdly, there are fewer swing voters due to the deeper polarization of the country. Some experts describe the electorate as calcified. This midterm election first and foremost determines whether the Republican Party can sustain its dominant political position it has enjoyed over the past two years, during which it has held sway over the executive branch, Congress and the Supreme Court. The outcome will also decide whether congressional Democrats can impose greater checks on Trump for the remainder of his term. It also signals whether Democrats will use Congress as a platform to further stoke partisan rifts and fuel escalating bipartisan conflict in the next two years, Wu Xinbo, Dean of the Institute of International Studies of Fudan University, told the Global Times. Three plausible scenarios loom for the US' polarized electoral landscape: a divided Congress, Democratic majorities across both chambers, or sustained Republican control of Capitol Hill, said Zhang Jiadong, professor at the Center for American Studies, Fudan University. Unlike presidential contests, midterm elections center on congressional and gubernatorial races, with voter priorities varying sharply across states. Immigration dominates debates in some jurisdictions, while others prioritize prices, inflation, or Middle East-related foreign policy, said the expert. The midterm results may significantly reshape the current administration's domestic policy operating environment over the coming two years, without necessarily altering the fundamental trajectory of its foreign policy, Zhang noted. Midterm elections typically center on domestic issues, yet this one is different, Wu said, adding that its result is likely to exert a marked impact on US foreign policy and international dynamics, with repercussions concentrated in the Middle East.

item.title: When Nazi symbol becomes a Halloween prop in Japan
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-02 22:39:00
Illustration: Chen Xia/GT Halloween is a time for dressing up, but not every symbol makes for a fun costume. This year's Halloween in Japan brought the issue into focus. On Saturday evening, a post on the X platform drew widespread attention. The photos showed multiple Japanese participants displaying the Nazi swastika. The account was later temporarily suspended for violations of the platform's rules on hateful content. But the photos continued to circulate, drawing criticism from users around the world. Some comments were blunt: "So this is what peace loving nation Japan looks like." Others pointed out: "Japan NEVER paid for its war crimes," "A lot of Japanese ppl dont learn modern history from schools. It is very hard to make them understand why what they are doing over there is wrong." The situation points to a question: Why do such symbols seem to have lost much of their historical weight for some young Japanese people? As early as 2014, The Guardian ran a report on two key politicians of then Japanese cabinet who had been photographed smiling with Kazunari Yamada, the leader of a Japanese neo-Nazi group. Sanae Takaichi, then internal affairs minister, was one of them. Although she later tried to distance herself from Yamada, the fact that such a photo could be taken at all, had already exposed how loosely the lines were drawn between Japan's right-wing political establishment and neo-Nazi circles. The deeper problem lies in the state-led shaping of historical memory. The Japanese government has continued to revise history textbooks. This is no longer simply a matter of downplaying the past. It amounts to a systematic effort to erase the memory of wartime atrocities. In the latest high school textbooks, terms such as "comfort women" and "forced labor" have been replaced with expressions such as "recruited" and "mobilized." Descriptions of "aggression" are nowhere to be found, and relevant chapter titles have been changed to the so-called "The Manchurian Incident and the Rise of the Military." The history books children grow up reading are themselves designed to sidestep the central question: What did Japan actually do? Outside the classroom, popular culture does something else: It turns historical symbols into entertainment. Anime, video games, films and television dramas pull symbols out of their bloody historical context and turn them into material that can be collected, worn and consumed. Once a symbol is reduced to a "cool-looking design" on a piece of clothing, its moral weight is stripped away. In 2016, the Japanese idol group Keyakizaka46 faced international backlash after wearing outfits resembling Nazi uniforms. During the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar, Japanese fans were stopped by security personnel from displaying Rising Sun flags in the stands. These incidents point to the same question: Why does Japanese society repeatedly find itself embroiled in similar controversies whenever symbols linked to its wartime past appear? Germany offers a stark contrast. Under German law, publicly displaying symbols linked to Nazi organizations is a criminal offense. Violations can result in a fine or up to three years in prison. Japan has no comparable legal boundary. And worse, many people, including high-level politicians, continue to worship at notorious Yasukuni Shrine, which enshrines Class-A war criminals from WWII. Over time, the next generation has grown increasingly detached from the idea that the bloody history must be remembered. The real danger is not the mere appearance of these symbols, but the gradual loss among young Japanese people of any sense of the evil they represent. When Nazi symbols can be casually turned into Halloween props, what this reveals is not simply the ignorance of a few individuals, but a systemic distortion of historical understanding. In the minds of some young Japanese people, the gravity of aggression, genocide and responsibility for war has been hollowed out. The swastika displayed in Japan during Halloween is merely one visible fragment of a much larger problem. And it's a warning that when distortions of historical memory are repeatedly tolerated, they eventually become a systematic erosion of our shared understanding of the past. Japan has long sought to diminish the weight of its own wartime crimes. When it invaded and brutally ravaged Asia, it called its aggression "liberation." The world, especially Asia, has watched this script play out before. It must not pretend it does not recognize the script.

item.title: China to launch third stock market swap operation as demand exceeds 100b yuan, signaling fresh efforts to bolster market stability: experts
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-02 21:52:00
The building of the China Securities Regulatory Commission in Beijing. Photo: VCG China's central bank announced on Monday that it will launch a third round of its stock market swap facility on Tuesday, a fresh move to support the stable and healthy development of the country's capital market. The latest operation is expected to channel more funds into the stock market by helping financial institutions expand their investment capacity, while broader participation by institutional investors could help strengthen market confidence, a Chinese expert said. The move came as the People's Bank of China (PBC), together with the National Financial Regulatory Administration (NFRA) and the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), announced further measures to optimize two policy tools supporting the capital market, including making the stock repurchase and shareholding increase relending program a long-term institutional arrangement and lowering its relending interest rate. According to an official announcement by the PBC on Monday, the third operation of the Securities, Funds and Insurance Companies Swap Facility (SFISF) will have a one-year term, which may be extended depending on circumstances. A total of 31 securities firms and fund management companies have submitted requests for the facility, with the total amount requested exceeding 100 billion yuan ($15 billion). The strong interest from financial institutions shows that the swap facility has gained broad recognition among market participants, Xi Junyang, a professor at the Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, told the Global Times on Monday. By allowing institutions to exchange eligible assets for highly liquid assets that can be used to obtain financing, the facility could bring additional funds into the stock market. Greater participation could also help strengthen market confidence, the Shanghai-based industry analyst said. The PBC, together with the NFRA and the CSRC, held two separate meetings on Monday with securities, fund and insurance companies and banks to review progress in implementing the two policy tools, hear financial institutions' opinions and suggestions, and discuss how to make fuller use of the tools to support capital market stability. The PBC said that the SFISF had been extended multiple times since its launch in October 2024, with its outstanding balance currently standing at 105 billion yuan. The facility has helped leverage the professional investment capabilities of securities, fund and insurance institutions and generated a broader demonstration effect, according to the central bank. The stock repurchase and shareholding increase relending program has also made important progress. According to the PBC, loan agreements signed under the policy have reached about 440 billion yuan, while cumulative loan disbursements have exceeded 280 billion yuan, helping meet listed companies' financing needs for managing their market capitalization. In a significant policy adjustment, the stock repurchase and shareholding increase relending program will be shifted from a temporary arrangement to a long-term institutional arrangement, while the relending interest rate will be lowered from 1.25 percent to 1 percent. Financial institutions are expected to adhere to market-oriented pricing principles, apply reasonable lending margins on top of the relending rate and expand loan disbursements under the program. For the SFISF, the authorities said that they would conduct operations at appropriate times, expand the number of participating institutions, appropriately lower swap fees and optimize collateral and operational arrangements. The PBC said that the two policy tools had gradually demonstrated their role in the capital market's internal stabilization, while financial institutions' awareness and capabilities in supporting market stability and listed companies' market capitalization management had continued to improve. The PBC previously conducted two SFISF operations, in October 2024 and January 2025, with transaction sizes of 50 billion yuan and 55 billion yuan. Each operation attracted bids from 20 institutions, according to the Securities Times. The latest operation comes against a backdrop of recent fluctuations in China's stock market. Chinese stocks rebounded on Monday, with the Shanghai Composite Index gaining 1.08 percent, the Shenzhen Component Index rising 1.63 percent and the ChiNext Index climbing 1.87 percent, according to Xinhua Finance. The upcoming operation reflects China's continued efforts to support a stable stock market, Li Chang'an, a professor at the Academy of China Open Economy Studies at the University of International Business and Economics, told the Global Times on Monday. "By encouraging institutions to invest more quickly and potentially lowering financing costs, the policy could bring more funds into the market, help reduce market volatility and boost investor confidence," said Li. Over the longer term, however, sustained capital market performance will still depend on improvements in the fundamentals of listed companies and stronger investor confidence, added Li.

item.title: China, Vietnam to hold second joint counter-terrorism exercise in Hanoi
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-02 20:44:00
The China-Vietnam joint counter-terrorism training is underway, in Nanning, South China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region on July 27, 2024. File photo: Xinhua The Chinese People's Armed Police Force and the mobile police force under the Vietnamese Ministry of Public Security are set to conduct a joint counter-terrorism exercise, codded "Cooperation-2026," in Hanoi, Vietnam, in early to mid-November, China's Ministry of National Defense announced on Monday. The exercise, themed around joint efforts to "combat violent terrorist crimes," will cover a range of training subjects, including explosive ordnance detection and disposal, ground maneuvering and assaults on high-rise buildings, according to the announcement. This will be the second exercise of its kind between the two countries and is expected to deepen exchanges and cooperation in counter-terrorism while enhancing their capabilities for joint operations, the ministry said. The inaugural exercise, held in 2024 in Southwest China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, was aimed at addressing shared concerns over terrorist threats and focused on joint efforts to combat violent terrorist activities, according to the Xinhua News Agency. During the two-week exercise, Chinese and Vietnamese personnel conducted training across seven categories and 27 subjects, including exchanges and discussions, command, skills, water-based operations, tactical coordination, specialized counterterrorism drills and comprehensive counterterrorism exercises. The program also featured sports competitions and cultural performances. Compared with the inaugural exercise, this year's training will take place in Vietnam and focus on several key urban counter-terrorism operations, Wang Yunfei, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Monday. The first exercise covered a relatively broad range of subjects, including water-based training and comprehensive tactical drills across different scenarios. The upcoming exercise places greater emphasis on explosive ordnance disposal, ground maneuvering and building-entry operations, which are particularly relevant to counter-terrorism missions in complex urban environments, Wang said. The change of venue is also significant, as conducting the exercise in Hanoi will allow personnel from both sides to become more familiar with the operational environment in Vietnam and practice coordination under conditions closer to those they may encounter during actual counter-terrorism missions there, he noted. "The move also demonstrates growing mutual trust between the two sides," Wang said, adding that "training will also help improve coordination in command procedures, tactical cooperation and joint responses to security threats." "The two countries could also explore further cooperation in the application of unmanned equipment," Wang said. The program in 2024 featured a number of unmanned systems, including robotic dogs, biomimetic robotic birds and wall-climbing robots, which were used in coordinated operations. Virtual reality (VR) and mixed reality (MR) technologies were also employed to create simulated confrontation scenarios, according to the China Youth Daily. Such technologies have increasingly become important tools in counter-terrorism training, allowing personnel to practice responding to complex scenarios while improving coordination between human operators and unmanned platforms, said Wang, adding that the upcoming exercise could feature further technological upgrades, although its specific equipment and arrangements have yet to be announced. In his view, the selection of training subjects for the 2026 exercise also reflects the challenges posed by terrorist activities in densely populated urban areas, where high-rise buildings, complicated structures and potential explosive threats can make operations particularly difficult. Explosive ordnance disposal, rapid ground maneuvering and assaults on high-rise buildings address several key challenges in such scenarios, requiring participating personnel to improve their ability to respond quickly, coordinate movements and carry out precise operations in complex environments, he noted. Beyond the military and operational aspects, the exercise also carries broader significance for bilateral security cooperation. Against a backdrop of complex and evolving regional security challenges, closer counter-terrorism coordination between China and Vietnam will help the two countries strengthen their ability to address cross-border terrorist threats and transnational crimes, while contributing to security and stability in the region, Wang said. Looking ahead, the two sides could explore expanding cooperation into areas such as intelligence sharing, cross-border law enforcement operations, joint training involving unmanned equipment and emergency rescue, he added.

item.title: China to launch 5-10 joint archaeological projects with foreign partners in next five years, deepen Belt and Road cooperation
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-02 18:59:00
A mud-brick structure uncovered by a joint Chinese-Egyptian archaeological team at the Sekhmet Temple site in Egypt Photo: Courtesy of Shanghai Museum China will step up international archaeological cooperation over the next five years, with plans to develop five to 10 joint archaeological projects with foreign partners, particularly those in countries participating in the Belt and Road Initiative. The projects will serve as models for international cooperation, the National Cultural Heritage Administration (NCHA) said Monday. The measures are part of China's archaeological development plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-30), which was outlined at an NCHA press conference on Monday. The plan calls for improving the management system for joint archaeological projects and supporting Chinese archaeological institutions and universities in carrying out overseas excavations and engaging in academic exchanges. It also proposes joint archaeological research in the Austronesian-speaking world, the Himalayan region, and areas along the Silk Road and Maritime Silk Road, as well as studies of ancient Egyptian, Greek and Maya civilizations, according to a notice published on the website of the NCHA on Saturday. Ongoing fieldwork in Central Asia will remain an important part of the cooperation. Zhu Jiangsong, a member of the joint archaeological team from Northwest University's School of Cultural Heritage, told the Global Times that excavations at the Bandikhan II site in Uzbekistan would continue in the coming years. The joint Chinese-Uzbek team has also uncovered a 3,000-year-old city in Uzbekistan, offering new insights into urban planning and construction during the early Iron Age, he said. According to Zhu, the archaeological cooperation program includes training and fieldwork covering Chinese and Silk Road archaeology, cultural relics conservation, heritage management and archaeological science, bringing together scholars from both countries. Northwest University will also support the development of the China-Central Asia Belt and Road Joint Laboratory for Human and Environmental Studies and provide professional training for Uzbek specialists, Zhu said. The NCHA also announced that China will promote research into ancient Egyptian, Greek and Maya civilizations, and deepen cooperation with countries including Saudi Arabia, Tunisia, Egypt and Greece in underwater archaeology and cultural heritage protection, according to the notice. A recent example of such cooperation is the discovery of two sacred lakes at the Montu Temple precinct in Luxor, Egypt, by a joint Chinese-Egyptian archaeological team. The discovery marks the first layout of double sacred lake within a single ancient Egyptian temple precinct, Xinhua reported, citing the NCHA. During the 15th Five-Year Plan period, China will also strengthen its capacity for overseas joint archaeological research by promoting long-term partnerships between domestic archaeological institutions and universities and their foreign counterparts, according to the NCHA. The plan also calls for strengthening Northwest University's Collaborative Research Center for Archaeology of the Silk Roads to support international academic cooperation, the NCHA notice said. Fu Zengqi, a member of the Silk Road Archaeology Research Center, told the Global Times that ongoing projects include multiple excavations in Uzbekistan. Other projects that have completed this year's fieldwork include excavations at the Shorobashat ancient city site in Kyrgyzstan and Pazyryk culture burial sites in Russia's Altai region, Fu said. Wang Jianxin, director of Northwest University's Silk Road Archaeology Research Center, said his team began working with the Institute of Archaeology of the Uzbekistan Academy of Sciences in 2013, the year the Belt and Road Initiative was proposed. That partnership marked the start of a growing program of joint archaeological research between China and Uzbekistan. In addition to cooperation with universities such as the National University of Uzbekistan, China's archaeological engagement in Central Asia has since expanded into a broader, multilateral framework, said Wang. "Through the Belt and Road Initiative, Northwest University's archaeology program will continue to build on its long-standing academic tradition of Silk Road studies and play an active role in deepening understanding of the history and cultural traditions of countries and regions along the route, fostering mutual understanding between China and its partners, and promoting closer people-to-people ties," Wang said.

item.title: China's top procuratorate highlights doxxing, celebrity data leaks and other personal information crimes
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-02 14:32:00
Photo: VCG China's top procuratorate on Monday released a set of typical cases involving infringements of citizens' personal information, including doxxing-fueled cyber harassment and fandom malpractices. The cases released by China's Supreme People's Procuratorate (SPP), eight in total, illustrate emerging trends in crimes involving citizens' personal information. One case involving doxxing and cyber-related harassment illustrates the harm caused at each stage of the criminal activity and the criminal charges that such conduct may carry. One disclosed case exposes how several defendants illegally obtained more than 16 million items of citizens' personal information including ID numbers and phone numbers. They also stole more than one billion records, including personal data such as registered accounts and contact numbers of users from multiple online forums and cloud storage spaces. In addition, the defendants used the illegally obtained personal information to dox and harass 47 victims across China, including online game players and online forum moderators, both online and offline. Five of the victims were minors. The defendants were handed prison terms ranging from nine months to four years and five months, plus fines. The cases also highlight misconduct within online fan communities. The SPP disclosed details of one case involving a 1990-born airline customer service worker surnamed Shu. She is also an avid fan active in online fandom groups, who exploited her work-related access to the airline's system to look up celebrities' flight information and sell it through the groups for illicit profits. Between October 2021 and April 2024, Shu used the airline's internal system to look up and sell flight information involving more than 100 flights taken by more than 30 celebrities, pocketing over 10,000 yuan (about $1,490) in illegal gains. She received a ten-month prison sentence, suspended for one year, and was fined 30,000 yuan for the crime of infringing upon citizens' personal information. The SPP said that for offences where lawbreakers illegally obtain and sell location data of celebrities, prosecutors pursue criminal liability in accordance with the law while filing incidental civil public-interest litigation to hold those responsible civilly liable. Another case highlights criminal acts committed under the guise of private investigation, in which GPS tracking technology was abused to unlawfully obtain citizens' personal information and violate their personal and property rights. Other cases involve offenders targeting older people who have limited online literacy and a weak awareness of how to protect themselves. The SPP stressed that relevant authorities should carry out proactive legal outreach to help seniors bolster their risk awareness and defensive capabilities. Besides, the released cases include personal information infringements linked to telecom fraud, fraudulent online recruitment and unlawful acquisition of medical and health data. In the next phase, while continuing to punish illegal and criminal acts infringing upon citizens' personal information in accordance with the law, procuratorial organs will deepen inter-agency coordination and take a comprehensive approach to governance, the SPP said.
